THOUGHT: The patient has lifelong/night-blindness from childhood with otherwise well-preserved central acuity and color vision. The ERG shows a flat rod response with reduced amplitudes over 30 years (progression of rod dysfunction) while photopic responses are relatively preserved — this localizes primarily to rod (peripheral) disease. Imaging (FAF and OCT) shows a well-demarcated superotemporal zone of photoreceptor and RPE loss with a narrow hyperautofluorescent margin; that retinal location corresponds to the inferonasal visual field scotoma on Goldmann testing (anatomic-field correlation). The lesion is sectoral rather than diffuse and the rest of the fundus lacks classic widespread bone‑spicule pigmentation, which is typical of a sectoral form of a rod‑cone dystrophy. The long history with slow progression of rod dysfunction argues against purely stationary disorders (e.g., classic Oguchi disease) and the few yellow spots could mimic flecks (fundus albipunctatus) but the progressive localized atrophy on OCT/FAF favors a progressive sectoral degenerative process.

Putting these findings together, the single best unifying diagnosis is a sectoral retinitis pigmentosa (sectoral rod‑cone dystrophy) affecting the superotemporal retina with corresponding inferonasal field loss. Top alternatives include generalized retinitis pigmentosa (early/minimal fundus changes), fleck dystrophies/fundus albipunctatus (stationary fleck disease with rod dysfunction), congenital stationary night blindness/Oguchi disease (rod dysfunction but typically nonprogressive and characteristic Mizuo–Nakamura sign), and metabolic/chorioretinal atrophies that can present with nyctalopia (e.g., gyrate atrophy).

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Sectoral retinitis pigmentosa (sectoral rod–cone dystrophy) — most likely
2. Generalized retinitis pigmentosa (rod–cone dystrophy), early/minimally pigmented stage
3. Fundus albipunctatus (fleck dystrophy with congenital night blindness) — less likely given progressive rod loss and localized atrophy
4. Congenital stationary night blindness / Oguchi disease — less likely because of progression and localized RPE/photoreceptor loss
5. Gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina (or other chorioretinal dystrophy) — less likely but can cause nyctalopia and localized chorioretinal atrophy
